14.1: I shall declare again the supreme knowledge, the best of all knowledge, knowing which sages have gone to the highest perfection.
14.2: Those who take refuge in this knowledge and reach My nature are not born at creation nor disturbed at dissolution.
14.3: My womb is the great nature; in it I place the seed, and from that comes the birth of all beings.
14.4: Whatever forms are produced in any womb, the great nature is their womb and I am the seed-giving father.
14.5: Sattva, rajas and tamas, born of nature, bind the imperishable dweller in the body.
14.6: Sattva, being pure, luminous and free from ill, binds by attachment to happiness and to knowledge.
14.7: Rajas is of the nature of passion, born of craving and attachment; it binds the embodied by attachment to action.
14.8: Tamas, born of ignorance, deludes all embodied beings; it binds by heedlessness, indolence and sleep.
14.9: Sattva attaches to happiness, rajas to action; tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches to heedlessness.
14.10: Sattva prevails by overpowering rajas and tamas; so with each in turn — the three take turns dominating.
14.11: When the light of knowledge shines through every gate of the body, know that sattva is predominant.
14.12: Greed, activity, undertaking of works, restlessness and longing arise when rajas is predominant.
14.13: Darkness, inertia, heedlessness and delusion arise when tamas is predominant.
14.14: If the embodied dies when sattva prevails, one attains the spotless worlds of the knowers of the highest.
14.15: Dying in rajas, one is born among those attached to action; dying in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
14.16: The fruit of good action is sattvic and pure; the fruit of rajas is pain, and of tamas ignorance.
14.17: From sattva knowledge is born, from rajas greed, and from tamas heedlessness, delusion and ignorance.
14.18: Those established in sattva go upward, the rajasic remain in the middle, the tamasic go downward.
14.19: When one sees no doer other than the gunas and knows what is beyond them, one attains My being.
14.20: Transcending the three gunas from which the body arises, the embodied is freed from birth, death, old age and pain, and attains immortality.
14.21: Arjuna asks the practical question: by what marks is one who has crossed the gunas known, and how does such a one behave?
14.22: Krishna answers: one who neither dislikes light, activity and delusion when present, nor longs for them when absent —
14.23: — who sits unconcerned, unmoved by the gunas, knowing that the gunas alone act, standing firm and not wavering —
14.24: — alike in pleasure and pain, self-abiding, regarding clod, stone and gold alike, the same to dear and unfriendly, firm, indifferent to praise and blame —
14.25: — the same in honour and dishonour, to friend and enemy, abandoning all undertakings: that one has transcended the gunas.
14.26: One who serves Me with unswerving devotion transcends the gunas and becomes fit to become Brahman.
14.27: For I am the abode of Brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of eternal dharma and of absolute bliss.
